findings: SOURCE TIER. `_MAXSDoorHandler.s`, 46,126 bytes of the author's own commented assembler, ships in the archive -- the SECOND extension in this corpus to arrive that way, after Explode, and again nothing in any catalogue said so. Labels, includes, structure offsets, and its own equates: `ExtNb equ 16-1`, `MsgLength equ 106`. REPLACES AN AMOSTOOLS STUB. Until 2026-08-12 this row held only the token table with the library stripped out from under it -- both length fields zero, no code, every routine word overwritten with `====` -- so the tier could not rise above `manual`. The real library's table is IDENTICAL to the stub's, entry for entry, id for id and spec for spec, which is a check on the AMOSTools reader as much as on this registration. What changes is that the code is now here to read. CAUTION, AND IT MATTERS FOR EVERY CITATION: the source is dated 3 January 1995 and the library 29 May 1994, EIGHT MONTHS EARLIER. They are not guaranteed to be the same build. Check the token table against the listing before treating a line of the source as a statement about this binary; where they disagree the binary is what programs ran against. WHAT IT IS FOR: 22 keywords that let an AMOS program be a door for MAX's BBS -- `m_portopen`, `m_portclose`, `m_bbstext`, `m_localtext`, `m_modemchar`, `m_screenchar`, `m_bbschar`, `m_prompttext` and the rest. It is message-port plumbing over a 106-byte DoorMsg, which is why the source's second equate is that length. THE ARCHIVE IS ~200 FILES OF EVIDENCE: about twenty complete BBS doors written in AMOS by the same author -- AriSE, Nice_Chat, Sysop_door, Section_Mover, DirectDownLoad and the nine settings/ programs -- most with their .AMOS sources beside the compiled binaries. Programs written against a 22-keyword extension BY THE PERSON WHO WROTE IT are the best available statement of what the keywords are for. `Aridoorstuff.h` is the C-side header for the same protocol.
notes: Writes BBS doors for the MAXS bulletin board. Ships with the author's commented assembler source.
